alternatives.explanation: Confounding by stock and fulfilment (Simpson's paradox). Markdowns may go on discontinued units the branch actually holds (clearance), while discontinued SKUs quoted without a markdown are lines the branch doesn't stock and has to special-order. Those are two different sales, and pooling them could hide a large markdown effect.
alternatives.test: Rebuild stock on hand at quote time per SKU x branch as the running total of wms_inventory_transactions before the quote day (ASOF join). Split past-discontinued quote lines by in-stock vs not. Compare win rates with and without a markdown in each stratum and within SKU. Check how won lines were fulfilled.
alternatives.result: The original pooled numbers reproduce (q362: 0.4265 with markdown, 66,471 quotes; 0.4354 without, 64,922). Markdowns sit almost only on in-stock lines: 89.11% of lines with 1-10x the quoted qty on hand and 96.17% at 10x+, vs 4.82% where the branch had none (q377, 159,735 past-discontinued quote lines, 2016-2025). Won no-markdown, no-stock lines were mostly special orders (30,293 special, 3,522 short, 1,177 transfer). Won marked-down in-stock lines were filled from stock (31,985) (q388). On single-line quotes within SKU, the markdown effect is +0.2892 in stock (win 0.438 with a markdown, 14,010 quotes, vs 0.1551 without, 1,625 quotes; 155 SKUs) and -0.2932 out of stock (864 vs 7,535 quotes, 112 SKUs) (q386). Within SKU x year x branch for in-stock lines it is +0.3252 (468 cells, 2,354 vs 1,187 quotes, q396). The finding's -0.0022 within-customer and -0.0044 within-SKU figures average two opposite effects. Caveat: the 864 'no stock' lines that were marked down were mostly filled from stock (837 of them, q388), so my stock measure misclassifies some lines. The in-stock contrast is the cleaner one.

alternatives.explanation: Misleading dose-response. A flat win rate across markdown depths could hide a step between none and any, and depth is confounded with how long ago the SKU was discontinued.
alternatives.test: Win rate by markdown depth within in-stock, single-line, past-discontinued quotes, with average months since discontinued_on. Also time since discontinuation across all past-discontinued lines.
alternatives.result: In stock: 0.1543 with no markdown (1,640 quotes) vs 0.4402 / 0.4342 / 0.4464 / 0.4396 at <20% / 20-30% / 30-40% / 40%+ (2,924 / 562 / 1,165 / 11,315 quotes) (q393). The effect is a step: any markdown restores a normal win rate. Depth tracks age: average 4.6 months since discontinuation at <20% and 66.2 months at 40%+ (q393). Depth also rises with age across all lines, from 0.0606 average at <3 months to 0.42 at 24+ months (q370), which looks like a schedule. Flat depth-response says nothing about whether markdowns win. It suggests that shallower markdowns might do as well, but depth and age move together, so I can't separate them.

alternatives.explanation: The money: is $3.16M a year margin given away, and is it recoverable?
alternatives.test: Re-derive the figure. Compare marked-down won-quote prices to product unit_cost. Compare with markdowns on all sales-order lines. Scale by the in-stock win ratio.
alternatives.result: The arithmetic holds: $9,489,254.54 of markdown on won quotes in 2023-2025 (q397), averaging $3,163,084.85 a year (q405; the original's .84 is a rounding difference). That is markdown against list x (1 - discount), not lost margin. Marked-down won lines sold below unit_cost: 100% of lines in 2016-2022 and 79.22% in 2023-2025. Gross margin on those lines in 2023-2025 was -$4,174,119.06, against $5,733,277.62 had they sold without a markdown (q397). The pricing looks like clearing stock at or below cost. Without a markdown, in-stock quotes win 0.351 times as often (q405). Even if the step were causal, at most about $1,110,245.66 a year of the $3.16M is markdown on sales that would likely have happened anyway (q405, illustrative only). The rest of those sales would probably have been lost, leaving discontinued stock unsold. Separately, quotes are only part of markdown activity: all sales-order lines with markdowns carried an implied $58,552,796.44 over 2016-2025, and 42.54% sold below cost (q366, 84,092 lines). Median price/cost on those lines was 1.0785 (q373).

alternatives.explanation: Rep spread is noise plus customer composition rather than a rep effect. The finding's interpretation; tested here directly rather than through split-half correlations, which are weak with 36 reps.
alternatives.test: Check whether customers are ever reassigned. Estimate between-customer variance of trade x branch-adjusted win rates. Compare the observed quote-weighted variance of rep residuals with what customer heterogeneity (weighted by each rep's customer concentration) plus binomial noise would produce.
alternatives.result: Every quote's rep_id and branch equal the customer's assigned rep and branch (551,951 quotes, 5,602 customers, q364), so rep and customer can't be separated by reassignment. Observed rep-residual variance is 0.0003011 (SD 0.0174), against 0.0002764 (SD 0.0166) expected from customer heterogeneity and sampling alone (customer variance 0.00499; reps hold 46-286 customers). The excess SD is about 0.005 (q401, q405). This supports the finding's rep conclusion, more strongly than the finding stated it. The 0.6459 time-half correlation is what you'd expect when the same customers appear in both halves.

alternatives.explanation: Is the no-markdown-while-in-stock pattern a few reps' practice? If so, the in-stock contrast could be a rep effect rather than a markdown effect.
alternatives.test: Share of in-stock past-discontinued quote lines without a markdown, by rep.
alternatives.result: Spread across all 36 reps: 0.0596-0.1486, median 0.0955, at least 74 lines each (80,678 lines, q408). Not concentrated in a few reps. Why those lines carry no markdown is not recorded.

what_changed: The headline claim, that markdowns buy no wins, is reversed once stock on hand is accounted for. It came from pooling stocked clearance lines with special-order lines. Within SKU x year x branch for stocked discontinued equipment, marked-down quotes win 0.3252 more often (q396). Without a markdown, stocked discontinued equipment wins 0.1543 vs about 0.44 with any markdown (q393). The $3.16M a year is arithmetically right but is not margin given away: those lines already sold mostly below unit_cost (q397), and most of the sales would likely not have happened without the markdown. The proposed pilot (quote discontinued equipment at customer discount only) would, on this evidence, cut win rates on stocked discontinued equipment sharply. The rep-spread half survives and is strengthened: residual rep spread after trade x branch is close to what customer composition and noise alone produce (q401).
revised_conclusion: Retracted as stated. The markdown claim and its $3.16M a year size and action don't hold. Revised markdown finding (observed): markdowns on post-discontinued equipment are applied almost only when the branch holds the stock (q377). They are priced at or below unit cost (q397), and they coincide with a step from about 0.15 to about 0.44 in win rate within the same SKU, year and branch (q393, q396). Interpretation: this looks like a working clearance mechanism, not a giveaway. It may be partly selection, since why some stocked lines go unmarked is not recorded, so this is not proof that markdowns cause the wins. Depth may be more than needed (any depth wins about equally), but depth and stock age move together, so a test would have to vary depth at a fixed age. The rep half holds: raw rep win rates mislead. After trade x branch the spread (SD 0.0174) is close to the 0.0166 expected from which customers a rep holds plus noise (q401), and customers are never reassigned (q364), so the data can't show a rep effect separate from customers. Compare reps only within trade x branch at the customer level. This could stand as its own finding.
not_evidence_of: That markdowns cause wins: the in-stock contrast could reflect unrecorded reasons a rep skipped the markdown (for example a customer who wanted the new model). That the markdown depth is right: 40%+ sits on stock about 66 months past discontinuation, and shallower depths can't be tested at the same age. That the quote-level dollars are the whole markdown picture: most markdown flows through sales orders not linked to quotes (q366). That clearance is profitable: unit_cost is static, so the below-cost result compares to original cost, not current value. Holding cost and write-off value are not in the data. That reps make no difference: an excess SD of about 0.005 can't be ruled out, and without reassignment history the effects can't be separated. Nothing here is about any individual rep.
